```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_scip <- requireNamespace("scip", quietly = TRUE)
has_osqp <- requireNamespace("osqp", quietly = TRUE)
has_nloptr <- requireNamespace("nloptr", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(optcompR)
```

optcompR describes an optimization problem once, as variables, expressions,
constraints and an objective, and then classifies it, chooses a capable solver
```{r, include = FALSE}
has_z3r <- requireNamespace("z3r", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_z3r)
```

Numerical solvers work in floating point with tolerances. For linear models
(LP and MILP) the z3r package gives access to Z3, whose linear integer and
real arithmetic is a decision procedure: its answers `sat` and `unsat` are
exact statements about the model as written.

These functions need z3r and the Z3 library
(`remotes::install_github("adamrsophie/z3r")`).

## Exact feasibility

```{r}
m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", type = "integer", lower = 0, upper = 10)
opt_constraint(m, 2 * x == 7)
opt_z3_check(m)
```

No integer solves $2x = 7$, and Z3 proves it. A satisfying assignment is a
feasible point, not an optimal one:

```{r}
m2 <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m2, "x", type = "integer", lower = 0, upper = 10)
y <- opt_variable(m2, "y", lower = 0)
opt_constraint(m2, 2 * x + 0.1 * y == 7)
opt_objective(m2, y)
opt_z3_check(m2)
opt_z3_check(m2, objective_bound = 9.99)$status
```

The second call proves that no feasible point has $y \le 9.99$: because
$x \le 3$ is forced, $y = 70 - 20x \ge 10$.

## Certifying an optimum

`opt_z3_certify()` asks whether any feasible point beats the solver's
objective by more than a tiny relative margin. `unsat` proves the reported
value optimal for the model.

```{r}
k <- opt_model("max")
a <- opt_variable(k, "a", type = "binary")
b <- opt_variable(k, "b", type = "integer", lower = 0, upper = 3)
opt_constraint(k, a + b <= 4)
opt_objective(k, 3 * a + 2 * b)
r <- opt_solve(k)
opt_z3_certify(r)$certified
```

If the reported value were wrong, Z3 returns a better point as a
counterexample:

```{r}
bad <- r
bad$objective_value <- 8
opt_z3_certify(bad)[c("certified", "better_point")]
```

## Coefficients

Coefficients are doubles. With `coefficients = "decimal"` (the default),
`0.1` means exactly $1/10$; with `"binary"` it means the exact binary value
of the double, $3602879701896397 / 2^{55}$.

## What Z3 is not used for

Only linear models are translated. Z3's nonlinear real arithmetic is
incomplete and its semantics differ from numerical optimization, so
quadratic and nonlinear models are refused rather than sent to Z3.
Certification proves the optimal value, not exact feasibility of the
floating point solution vector. Exact solving can be slow for large integer
models.
